1) Stop the water (do this immediately if you can):
- If the toilet is still running: remove the tank lid and push the flapper (rubber piece at the bottom of the tank) down to stop water flowing, or lift the float up to stop filling.
- If it won’t stop: turn the shutoff valve behind/under the toilet clockwise until it stops turning.
- If you can’t find or turn that valve: if safe, shut off the main water for the home.

2) Contain the mess:
- Unplug anything electrical on the floor nearby.
- Use towels to block doorways/vents so water doesn’t spread to other rooms.
- Mop up standing water, especially near floor edges or upstairs bathrooms (to avoid leaks to the floor below).

I can get an emergency plumber dispatched, but I need a few details:

1) Full address (including city and ZIP/postcode):
2) What type of place is this? (apartment/condo, single-family house, business, etc.)
3) Is water still actively coming out, or is it now stopped but the floor is flooded?
4) How soon do you need someone? (Right now / within a few hours / today)
5) Any preference? (cheapest available / highest rated / doesn’t matter, just fastest)

Reply with those and I’ll match you with emergency plumbers and start the booking process right away.</action>

<action type="say">
Here are practical scripts you can use.

1) What to tell / ask the plumber (you can read this to them)

Describe the situation:
- “We’re in a multi-floor office building with shared restrooms on this floor.”
- “One toilet overflowed in the [men’s/women’s/unisex] restroom. We shut off the toilet’s supply valve so water has stopped.”
- “There was enough water to cover part of the bathroom floor, but we’re containing and cleaning it now.”
- “These restrooms share a main line with other bathrooms on this floor.”

Ask them to check:
- “Can you confirm if this is just a problem with this one toilet, or a blockage/issue in the main line for this floor?”
- “Please check other fixtures on this line (other toilets, sinks, floor drain) to make sure there isn’t a partial blockage.”
- “Do you see any signs of backflow from the main stack or vent issues?”
- “Is it safe to put this toilet and the rest of the fixtures back into normal use once you’re done?”

Ask for recommendations:
- “What caused the overflow (foreign object, blockage, mechanical failure, etc.), as best you can tell?”
- “Do you recommend any preventative work (e.g., main line jetting, replacing this toilet or flush mechanism, regular maintenance schedule)?”

Ask for documentation on their paperwork:
- “On the invoice or work order, can you please note:
  - your opinion of the cause,
  - whether the main line was affected,
  - what you did (e.g., cleared blockage, tested other fixtures),
  - whether you saw any signs of damage or risk outside the restroom?”
- “If you notice any water intrusion beyond the restroom (walls, hallway, or ceiling below), please point it out so we can report it.”

2) What to tell building management (email/message template)

You can adapt this:

Subject: Toilet Overflow – [Floor #] Restroom at 123 Tech Park Drive

“Hi [Name/Building Management],

We had a toilet overflow in the [men’s/women’s/unisex] restroom on the [Xth] floor at approximately [time]. We shut off the toilet’s supply valve, so the water is no longer running.

Current situation:
- Water spread across part of the restroom floor; we’ve contained it and started basic cleanup.
- This restroom is part of the shared main line serving the floor.
- We have called an emergency plumber to:
  - determine if this was a localized toilet issue or a main-line problem,
  - check other fixtures on the same line,
  - identify any potential impact on adjacent areas (walls, hallway, ceiling below).

Requests / next steps:
- Please arrange or confirm appropriate cleaning and disinfection of the affected area, and inspection for any water damage (including the ceiling/space below and adjacent walls).
- Let us know if you prefer to use your own plumbing vendor or restoration/cleaning services, or if you want to coordinate with the plumber we’ve contacted.
- We will share the plumber’s report/invoice, including their findings on cause, whether the main line was involved, and any preventative recommendations.

The affected restroom is currently closed and marked out of service until it’s inspected and cleared.

Thanks,
[Your Name]
[Your Company/Suite]
[Contact info]”

3) What you should document yourself

- Times:
  - When the overflow was noticed.
  - When you shut off the valve.
  - When you called the plumber and building management.
- Photos:
  - Overall bathroom floor showing where the water reached.
  - Base of walls, door threshold, and any nearby hallway if water approached it.
  - If possible later, any staining/damage on the ceiling below.
- People and vendors:
  - Name of the plumbing company and technician.
  - Names/times of anyone you spoke with in building management.

If you’d like, paste your actual draft email to building management and I can quickly edit it to be clearer or more formal.</action>
